103, 641, 642/2024 890/2023, 1255 & 1256/2024 following writ appeals have been filed by the Medical Services Recruitment Board (MRB) against the orders dated 23.03.2023 and 06.06.2023 passed in respective W.P.(MD).Nos. 5721, 5503, 5918, 4882, 6087, 6083 & 7224 of 2023.
5.

The essential facts necessary for the disposal of the writ appeals are discussed hereunder:-
5.1.

The appellants herein is the Medical Services Recruitment Board (MRB),
Chennai who issued notification inviting applications from eligible candidates for direct recruitment to the post of Food Safety Officer on temporary basis in Tamil Nadu Food Safety and Drug Administration Department.

The Commissioner, Tamil Nadu Food Safety and drug administration department, Chennai has sent proposals to fill up to fill up 131 posts as per Food Safety Subordinate Service rules and the same was approved by the Government in G.O.(D).No.975, Health and Family Welfare (M1) Department dated 27.08.2021 and thereafter notification dated 13.10.2021 came to be published by the Medical Services Recruitment Board (MRB).
https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis
The Respondents herein are the medical practitioners holding degrees in Siddha medicine and BDS(Bachelor of Dental Surgery).The
applications submitted by the respondents were accepted and they were permitted to take a written examination on 20.10.2022.
However, their names were omitted from the selection list published by the Board on the ground that degrees in Siddha Medicine and BDS does not fall within the definition of a degree in medicine.
Aggrieved by such exclusion, the respondents filed writ petitions challenging the impugned selection list.

6. Out of the writ appeals under consideration, W.A(MD).No. 641 and 642 of 2024 relates specifically to the exclusion of candidates holding a Bachelor of Dental Surgery(BDS) degree, while the remaining appeals pertain to the exclusion of candidates possessing degrees in Siddha Medicine.

7. With respect to W.A(MD).Nos. 102, 103, 641, 642, 1256 of 2024 & 890 of 2023, the learned counsel appearing for the appellants submitted that as per the educational qualification prescribed in the notification dated https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis ( Uploaded on: 09/12/2025 08:15:10 pm ) W.A.(MD).Nos.102, 103, 641, 642/2024 890/2023, 1255 & 1256/2024 13.10.2021, among the The Member Secretary vs S.Ganavel on 23 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16119482/
9
other qualification mentioned, the "Degree in Medicine" has been notified as one of the prescribed qualification for the post of food safety officer.

It is submitted by the learned counsel that as per Section 2(f) of the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956, the term "Medicine" means modern scientific medicine in all its branches and includes surgery and obstetrics, but does not include veterinary medicine and surgery, therefore, the said definition does not include other system of medicine such as Bachelor of Siddha in Medicine (BSMS)/M.D.(Siddha) and Bachelor of Dental Surgery(BDS).
7.1. In this regard, The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India have issued clarification in this regard on 12.10.2022.

"3.

In this context, for the purpose of qualification of Food Safety Officer specified in Rule 2.1.3(1) of Food safety and Standards Rules, 2011, it may be clarified that:-
i. The "degree" means the degrees as prescribed in Sub-section (3) of Section 22 of the University Grants Commission Act, 1956 (3 of 1956).

For the "Degree in Medicine", Hon'ble High Court of Allahabad in the matter of WP No. 2754 of 2015 Dr. Amit Pandey and ORs.

Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh and Ors observed that the degree in Medicine does not include any other system of medicine and it will not be proper to include or read any other degree awarded by councils under other acts in to degree of Medicine.
Medicine is defined only under Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 and not in other enactments.
iii. In respect of the "equivalent qualification", the Central Government has not notified any such equivalent qualification so far.

Hence, the only qualifications specified for the Food Safety Officer in the above-mentioned rules are applicable for the post of Food Safety Officer."
8.
It is also contended by the learned counsel for the appellants that the respondents qualifications viz., Bachelor of Siddha in Medicine (BSMS)/M.D. (Siddha), Bachelor of Dental Surgery(BDS)
cannot be treated as other equivalent /recognised qualification, as they have not been notified as equivalent/recognised qualification by the Central Government.

Since the respective respondents has not acquired the prescribed qualification for the post of Food Safety officer, they were not considered as eligible candidates under PSTM(Person studied in Tamil Medium) category.

The communication also clarified that these degrees are recognized medical qualifications under Section 2(h) and 35 of NCISM Act, 2020 and under section 2(f) and 35 of NCH https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis

9.1. It is also further contented that the 'degree in medicine' from a recognised University as a qualification prescribed is to be read and understood including all forms of medicine particularly the medicinal courses governed under the provisions of Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 and National Commission for Indian system of Medicine Act, 2020.

sentences.text: It is also stated that it cannot be denied for the reason that the course which the respondents underwent is neither scientific nor modern.

It is to be noted that the duration of course, the prescribed training period, the subject taught and the syllabus covered are all scientific studies borne out of Research and absorbing modern techniques.

9.2. The learned counsel for the respondent relied on the similar recruitment notification which came to be issued by the Public service Commission of the State of Tripura, where the educational qualification for the post of Food Safety Officer was prescribed as follows:-

Therefore, the said Degree comes under the category "Medicine".

9.3. In support of the arguments placed, the respondent placed reliance on Judgment passed by the Maharashtra Administrative Tribunal, Mumbai Bench in Original Application Nos. 322, 360, 361 & 370 of 2023, wherein the government considered that Ayurveda is not Medicine and the degree in BAMS is not a degree in Medicine,
but the tribunal interpreted the term "Medicine"
and held that the said term must be understood with fullest meaning.
Relying on this, the learned counsel for the Respondent prayed to dismiss the writ appeal and allow the respondents to be considered to the post of Food Safety Officer.

In this connection, the subject matter expert has reviewed the objections to two questions from an exam and has provided justifications for the correct answers.
For Question 16 (Batch-1): The correct answer is option 'C'- Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC).
The expert's justification is that while PVC is a widely used plastic, it can be harmful to human health.
Specifically, when melted, it releases a corrosive and toxic gas.
For Question 62 (Batch-1): The correct answer is option 'A'-100 ppm.
The expert clarifies that this is the correct answer based on the Prevention of Food Adulteration (PFA) Rules, 1955.
They also noted that the rules from 1954 might have different sweetener limits, but the correct answer for this specific question is 100 ppm as per the 1955 rules. ?

10.1. The learned counsel for the appellant also submitted that a total of 120 candidates were provisionally selected for the post of Food Safety Officer, following a certificate verification process on 23rd and 24th March, 2023.
The said list was published on 13.03.2023.

The cut-off mark for the last candidate selected under the General Turn (GT) category was 77.76 and the cut-off mark for the last candidate selected under the Backward Class Muslim (BCM) https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis
1256/2024 category was 74.97.
The respondent's score is 69.37 marks who belong to the Scheduled Caste (SC) category, whereas the last candidate selected under the SC category secured 70.12 marks.

Since, the respondent's score is lower than the SC category cut-off mark, the respondent had not reached the selection zone and thereby prayed for setting aside the order passed by the learned single Judge directing to award marks for the same and consequently directing the appellants to re-visit the selection process in favour of the respondent.
10.2.

Per contra, the learned counsel for the Respondent asserts that for Question No.16 Option (C)
petroleum is the correct answer as petroleum is a raw material and therefore cannot be used for wrapping sweets.

But the expert's provided answer, "Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC)" Option A, is incorrect because PVC can be used for wrapping sweets, as stated in the Food Safety and Standards Packaging Regulations 2018, specifically in Schedule-IV.

sentences.text: For Question No. 62, it is asserted that this question is flawed because it asks for a single maximum limit for artificial sweeteners in carbonated water and soft drinks.
However, according to the PFA Rules 1955, different artificial sweeteners have different maximum limits.

13.2. From the above observation, upon perusing the relevant rules for the post of Food Safety Officer, the qualification for food safety officer is set out under Rule 2.1.3 of the Food Safety and Standard Rules, 2011 "Rule 2.1.3: Food Safety Officer https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis

Qualification: Food Safety Officer shall be a whole time officer and shall, on the date on which he is so appointed possesses the following:
(i) [a Bachelor's or Master's or Doctorate degree in Food Technology or Dairy Technology or Biotechnology or Oil Technology or Agricultural Science or Veterinary Sciences or Bio-Chemistry or Microbiology or Chemistry or medicine from a recognized University, or ]
(ii) any other equivalent/recognized qualification [notified by the Food Authority with the prior approval of the Central Government], and (iii) has successfully completed training as specified by the Food Authority in a recognized institute or Institution approved for the purpose.
Provided that no person who has any financial interest in the manufacture, import or sale of any article of food shall be appointed to be a Food Safety Officer under this rule"
The rule indicates that for qualifying for the post of Food safety officer, one must hold the above said specifications, which includes "Degree in Medicine from a Recognised University".

The term "Medicine" as defined in the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956 under Section 2(f) which reads as "'Medicine' means modern scientific medicine in all its branches and includes surgery and obstetrics, but does not include veterinary medicine and surgery."

From the above definitions, the position that emerges is that as rightly observed by the learned single Judge, Section 2(f) of the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956, which defined 'medicine' has expressly excluded 'Veterinary medicine and surgery'.

By contrast, Rule 2.1.3 of the Food Safety and Standards Rules, 2011 includes 'Veterinary Sciences' as one of the prescribed qualifications for appointment as Food Safety Officer, along with other science degrees.
This makes it clear that the Rule was intended to provide a wider field of eligibility and is not tied down to the restrictive meaning of medicine under the 1956 Act.

If the Rule The Member Secretary vs S.Ganavel on 23 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16119482/
14 were confined to that definition
, Veterinary Sciences would not have found place at all.

Therefore,
the expression degree in medicine under Rule 2.1.3 must be understood in a broader sense, covering science and medical graduates as expressly specified in the Rule.

13.3. As rightly observed by the learned Judge, The Siddha system of medicine and its relevance is visible even today, through the role played by Siddha practitioners during the COVID-19 crisis and government-promoted remedies like 'Kabasura Kudineer and Nilavembu Dengue Kashayam'.

The value of any medical system, ancient or modern, depends on whether it is current, practical, and capable of serving the people.
It is the responsibility of the State to ensure that Siddha medicine remains relevant and effective.

In view of the same, this court is of the opinion that the term medicine should not be confined to either modern or traditional streams.

Limiting it to modern medicine alone would amount to a rigid and mechanical interpretation, creating arbitrary discrimination against holders of traditional medical degrees which would be inconsistent with principles of equality in service law.
The said term 'medicine' inherently embraces all branches of medicine.
Moreover, the role of a Food Safety Officer is not limited to medical expertise alone.
The graduates in Agricultural Science, Veterinary Science, Biochemistry, Microbiology, and Chemistry are also explicitly recognized under Rule 2.1.3.
Consequently, medicine must be interpreted in its fullest and most inclusive sense, reflecting both legislative intent and functional practicality.

opennyai_summary.facts:
The appellants herein is the Medical Services Recruitment Board (MRB),
Chennai who issued notification inviting applications from eligible candidates for direct recruitment to the post of Food Safety Officer on temporary basis in Tamil Nadu Food Safety and Drug Administration Department.
However, their names were omitted from the selection list published by the Board on the ground that degrees in Siddha Medicine and BDS does not fall within the definition of a degree in medicine.
Aggrieved by such exclusion, the respondents filed writ petitions challenging the impugned selection list.
It is submitted by the learned counsel that as per Section 2(f) of the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956, the term "Medicine" means modern scientific medicine in all its branches and includes surgery and obstetrics, but does not include veterinary medicine and surgery, therefore, the said definition does not include other system of medicine such as Bachelor of Siddha in Medicine (BSMS)/M.D.(Siddha) and Bachelor of Dental Surgery(BDS).
In this context, for the purpose of qualification of Food Safety Officer specified in Rule 2.1.3(1) of Food safety and Standards Rules, 2011, it may be clarified that:-
i. The "degree" means the degrees as prescribed in Sub-section (3) of Section 22 of the University Grants Commission Act, 1956 (3 of 1956).
https://www.mhc.tn.gov.in/judis
opennyai_summary.arguments:
Therefore, the said Degree comes under the category "Medicine".
The learned Single Judge after perusing the materials placed had rightly directed to award marks for the same and consequently directed the appellants to re-visit the selection process in favour of the respondent.
opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It is pertinent to note that the main issue that has to be decided is that whether as per notification dated 13.10.2021, Graduation in Siddha Medicine (BSMS), Post Graduation in Siddha Medicine (MD) and BDS(Bachelor of Dental Surgery) would be included in the expression "Degree in Medicine" or not, for consideration of the respondents to the post of Food Safety Officer.
From the above definitions, the position that emerges is that as rightly observed by the learned single Judge, Section 2(f) of the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956, which defined 'medicine' has expressly excluded 'Veterinary medicine and surgery'.
By contrast, Rule 2.1.3 of the Food Safety and Standards Rules, 2011 includes 'Veterinary Sciences' as one of the prescribed qualifications for appointment as Food Safety Officer, along with other science degrees.
This makes it clear that the Rule was intended to provide a wider field of eligibility and is not tied down to the restrictive meaning of medicine under the 1956 Act.
If the Rule The Member Secretary vs S.Ganavel on 23 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/16119482/
14 were confined to that definition
, Veterinary Sciences would not have found place at all.
Therefore,
the expression degree in medicine under Rule 2.1.3 must be understood in a broader sense, covering science and medical graduates as expressly specified in the Rule.
13.3. As rightly observed by the learned Judge, The Siddha system of medicine and its relevance is visible even today, through the role played by Siddha practitioners during the COVID-19 crisis and government-promoted remedies like 'Kabasura Kudineer and Nilavembu Dengue Kashayam'.
In view of the same, this court is of the opinion that the term medicine should not be confined to either modern or traditional streams.
Limiting it to modern medicine alone would amount to a rigid and mechanical interpretation, creating arbitrary discrimination against holders of traditional medical degrees which would be inconsistent with principles of equality in service law.
The said term 'medicine' inherently embraces all branches of medicine.
Moreover, the role of a Food Safety Officer is not limited to medical expertise alone.
The graduates in Agricultural Science, Veterinary Science, Biochemistry, Microbiology, and Chemistry are also explicitly recognized under Rule 2.1.3.
